Meanwhile modern applications lean heavily on a database cache to reduce latency; cached rows sit in fast local memory, sparing the primary database from repeated reads. This simple layer often delivers dramatic speedups for read-heavy workloads under real peak traffic.

However caches introduce hard problems that teams routinely underestimate. Stale entries can serve wrong answers, and invalidation strategies grow tangled as schemas evolve; distributed setups add another layer of pain when nodes disagree about which copy is current. A cache that returns outdated balances or inventory counts may damage trust long before anyone notices failures.

Along with sizing limits, staff must watch invalidation logic; stall bugs and cold starts can hurt applications badly. A good tactic is to log hit ratios daily, alarm on drops, and audit warming jobs so hot data stays local.

Finally treat your cache as a system: measure it, test expiry paths, and document ownership until work is truly done.
